title: Tensor-Train Joint Modeling for Few-Step Masked Diffusion

paper.title: Tensor-Train Joint Modeling for Few-Step Masked Diffusion
paper.abstract: Abstract Discrete diffusion promises orders-of-magnitude faster generation than autoregressive (AR) models for sequential discrete data, yet its full potential of few-step generation has remained out of reach due to a fundamental structural limitation. The conditional-independence assumption underlying current discrete diffusion models introduces a systematic parallelization bias that compounds with the number of tokens unmasked per step, becoming severe in the few-step regime that fast generation requires. We address this with the first framework for explicit joint distribution modeling in discrete diffusion via tensor decomposition , which represents the conditional clean distribution as a low-rank tensor with controllable expressivity. The framework supports both Canonical Polyadic (CPD) and Tensor-Train (TTD) decompositions, and we identify a structural bias of TTD toward dependencies between nearby tokens, formalized through Oseledets’ theorem relating TT-rank to unfolding-matrix rank, which is well-suited to sequential data such as natural language and line notations for molecular data. To enable efficient generation, we present an iterative marginal inference procedure with specialization for predetermined position schedules. Our framework integrates into pretrained MDMs through lightweight fine-tuning, yielding substantial improvements in few-step generation at a fraction of the cost of training from scratch.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Discrete diffusion has emerged as a compelling alternative to AR models for generating sequential discrete data such as text and proteins ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Its key promise is parallel token generation, producing multiple tokens per step rather than one. Most notably, Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) have scaled to large language models ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) with competitive quality and faster generation. In practice, however, this speed potential remains unrealized, as pushing toward few-step generation systematically degrades sample quality. The root cause is structural; to remain tractable, discrete diffusion models represent the conditional clean distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) under the conditional-independence assumption p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) = ∏ i = 1 N p θ ​ ( x i | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{\theta}(x^{i}|\bm{x}_{t}) . This assumption introduces a systematic parallelization bias ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) when multiple tokens are unmasked simultaneously. The bias compounds with the number of tokens unmasked per step, becoming especially severe in the few-step regime that fast generation requires. Resolving this bias requires modeling the joint distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) explicitly. However, naïve joint modeling is infeasible since the joint over N N tokens with vocabulary size V V forms an N N -dimensional tensor with V N V^{N} entries. Some existing approaches therefore sidestep direct joint modeling, introducing latent factors that induce token correlations ( Hayakawa et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) or borrowing dependence from auxiliary autoregressive models ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Compared to AR-auxiliary approaches, our method models the joint distribution explicitly as a tractable parametric family within the discrete diffusion model itself, without requiring any external pretrained model. Also, compared to latent-variable approaches, our explicit parameterization is orthogonal to their implicit one, and the two can be combined for further gains. Concurrent work ( Li et al., 2026 ) addresses the same factorization barrier by augmenting the factorized neural output with a tractable probabilistic circuit prior, requiring manual structural design for sequential locality, whereas Tensor-Train decomposition provides the same tractability with a theoretically grounded locality bias. In this work, we introduce a framework that explicitly parameterizes the joint distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) via tensor decomposition ( Kolda and Bader, 2009 ) . Compared to prior work, our framework provides explicit joint modeling within the diffusion model itself, without relying on auxiliary models. Our contributions are four-fold. • First explicit joint modeling via tensor decomposition. To our knowledge, this is the first work to parameterize the conditional clean distribution of discrete diffusion via tensor decomposition, strictly generalizing standard MDMs as the rank-one case. • TTD for sequential structure. We develop the framework for both Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) ( Hitchcock, 1927 ) and Tensor-Train Decomposition (TTD) ( Oseledets, 2011 ) , identifying a structural bias of TTD toward dependencies between nearby tokens, formalized through Oseledets’ theorem relating TT-rank to unfolding-matrix rank. • Efficient sampling via marginal inference. Direct sampling from a joint of size V N V^{N} is intractable. We present a chain-rule procedure built on iterative marginal inference via caching and parallel prefix sums, with specialization for predetermined position schedules. • Lightweight fine-tuning of pretrained MDMs. Our framework integrates into pretrained MDMs through small architectural modifications initialized to preserve the marginal predictions, yielding substantial few-step improvements at a fraction of the cost of training from scratch. In experiments on text generation (OpenWebText ( Gokaslan et al., 2019 ) , LM1B ( Chelba et al., 2014 ) ) and molecule generation (QM9 ( Blum and Reymond, 2009 ; Rupp et al., 2012 ) ), our framework delivers substantial few-step improvements across multiple base models, including MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) and VADD ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . As predicted by our theory, TTD consistently outperforms CPD on these sequential domains, with the largest gains concentrated in the few-step regime. For instance, TTD-based fine-tuning of VADD reduces 8-step generative perplexity on OpenWebText by 32.7% over vanilla VADD, while being only 1.7% slower at 128 timesteps.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Several lines of work attempt to address the parallelization bias arising from the conditional-independence assumption in discrete diffusion. The central challenge is the exponential size of the joint distribution: an N N -token sequence over vocabulary V V admits V N V^{N} possible configurations, making direct modeling intractable. Auxiliary-model approaches distill dependency information from separately trained autoregressive models via copula-based reweighting ( Liu et al., 2025 ) or energy-based reweighting ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . While effective, these methods inherit the inference cost of an external model and become inapplicable in domains lacking strong AR models, such as generation of line notations for molecular data. Our framework, in contrast, requires no additional model. Latent-variable approaches introduce latent factors that induce token correlations through marginalization, either via a continuous mixing variable ( Hayakawa et al., 2025 ) or a VAE-style latent vector ( Xie et al., 2026 ) ; our explicit modeling is orthogonal to these implicit approaches and can be combined with them for further gains. Sampling strategies mitigate the bias without modifying the model, selecting positions via low-discrepancy schedules ( Besnier et al., 2025 ) or adaptively bounding the number of simultaneously unmasked tokens through entropy criteria ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2025 ) ; these strategies integrate naturally within our framework. Concurrent work ( Li et al., 2026 ) couples the factorized neural output with a tractable probabilistic circuit prior, addressing the same factorization barrier with a different parameterization. Although probabilistic circuits offer general-purpose tractable inference, they require manual structural design for sequential locality, whereas Tensor-Train decomposition provides the same tractability with a theoretically grounded locality bias ( Sec. 4.2 ), making it particularly suited to natural language and line notations for molecular data without further structural engineering. The parallelization bias has also been studied in the context of speculative decoding for autoregressive language models, where Basharin et al. (2025) were the first to apply Canonical Polyadic Decomposition for explicit token-wise dependency modeling. We extend this idea to discrete diffusion for the first time, with two main technical contributions beyond their work: (1) identifying Tensor-Train Decomposition as particularly suited to sequential structure, with a theoretically grounded inductive bias toward dependencies between nearby tokens; and (2) presenting an efficient sampling procedure that introduces minimal overhead when sampling from the joint distribution.

sections.heading: 3.1 Background: Masked Diffusion Models (MDM)
sections.text: A Masked Diffusion Model (MDM) ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) is a discrete diffusion model whose forward process is an absorbing process. The absorbing token is commonly referred to as the mask token m m and thus lends the model its name. The forward process maps the data distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) p(\bm{x}) to the prior distribution, which is a Dirac delta concentrated at the fully masked sequence 𝐦 = [ m , m , … , m ] \mathbf{m}=[m,m,\ldots,m] , as t t progresses from 0 0 to 1 1 . The model is trained to predict the original values of the masked tokens in a partially masked sequence, typically under an assumption of conditional independence across tokens. sections.heading: 3.2 Method Overview
sections.text: Despite the promising progress of masked diffusion models, a key limitation lies in the conditional-independence assumption ( Eq. 2 ) imposed on p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) , which introduces a systematic parallelization bias ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) that becomes especially severe in the few-step regime. Explicitly modeling the joint distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) , however, is fundamentally a problem of scale. In continuous diffusion, the joint admits a tractable parameterization as a multivariate Gaussian. In the discrete setting, by contrast, the joint corresponds to an N N -dimensional tensor of size V N V^{N} , which rapidly becomes intractable as the vocabulary size V V and the sequence length N N grow. To address this challenge, we propose to model p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) explicitly via tensor decomposition . In Sec. 4 , we investigate two decompositions particularly suited to this purpose—Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) ( Hitchcock, 1927 ) and Tensor-Train Decomposition (TTD) ( Oseledets, 2011 ) —both supporting efficient training and sampling with only O ⁡ ( V ​ N ) O(VN) memory. We describe how each parameterizes the joint distribution and how generation is carried out under it. Our analysis identifies a structural limitation of CPD that motivates the use of TTD, whose form is naturally aligned with dependencies between nearby tokens, a property especially well suited to sequential data such as natural language ( Ebeling and Pöschel, 1994 ) and line notations for molecular data. Note that either decomposition reduces to the standard marginal probability formulation ( Eq. 2 ) in the rank-one special case. To our knowledge, this is the first work introducing tensor decomposition to joint probability modeling in discrete diffusion.

sections.heading: 4 Joint Probability Modeling via Tensor Decomposition
sections.text: In this section, we describe how the joint distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) can be modeled using two tensor decompositions: Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD; Sec. 4.1 ) and Tensor-Train Decomposition (TTD; Sec. 4.2 ). We discuss the advantages of TTD over CPD in capturing dependencies between nearby tokens, a property crucial for many practical domains such as text and line notations for molecular data. Building on the formulations, Sec. 4.3 describes the sampling procedure under either decomposition. sections.heading: 4.3 Efficient Sampling via Iterative Marginal Inference
sections.text: The tensor-decomposed forms (CPD and TTD) of p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) admit efficient evaluation at any 𝒙 \bm{x} , so training proceeds identically to a standard MDM with the same NLL loss ( Eq. 3 ). Sampling, however, is nontrivial: naively sampling from p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) would require evaluating it at all V N V^{N} possible sequences, an exponential cost in the sequence length N N . For efficient sampling, we present a general procedure based on the chain rule, followed by a special case that exploits additional structure. The chain rule of probability decomposes the joint into a sequence of conditionals. For any ordering ( i 1 , … , i K ) (i_{1},\ldots,i_{K}) of the K K positions, p ⁡ ( x i 1 , … , x i K | 𝒙 t ) = ∏ j = 1 K p ⁡ ( x i j | x i 1 , … , x i j − 1 , 𝒙 t ) . p(x^{i_{1}},\ldots,x^{i_{K}}|\bm{x}_{t})=\prod_{j=1}^{K}p(x^{i_{j}}|x^{i_{1}},\ldots,x^{i_{j-1}},\bm{x}_{t}). (13) We can therefore sample the subsequence one position at a time by conditioning on previously sampled positions and repeatedly applying marginal inference . Specifically, given a set S ⊆ { 1 , … , N } S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\} of conditioned positions with values 𝒙 S := { x j } j ∈ S \bm{x}_{S}:=\{x^{j}\}_{j\in S} , we compute the marginal p ⁡ ( x i | 𝒙 S , 𝒙 t ) p(x^{i}|\bm{x}_{S},\bm{x}_{t}) at every unconditioned position i ∉ S i\notin S . Sampling the full sequence then proceeds by initializing S = ∅ S=\emptyset and iteratively (i) performing marginal inference, (ii) selecting a position i ∉ S i\notin S , (iii) sampling x i ∼ p ⁡ ( x i | 𝒙 S , 𝒙 t ) x^{i}\sim p(x^{i}|\bm{x}_{S},\bm{x}_{t}) , and (iv) adding i i to S S . The position selection in step (ii) can follow any logit-based strategy (e.g., top probability-based ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) or entropy-based ( Ye et al., 2025 ) selection). The number of tokens sampled in a single step can be either fixed or determined by an adaptive sampler such as EB-Sampler ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2025 ) . sections.text: While the method above samples one position at a time, in many settings—random ordering, fixed orderings such as left-to-right — the positions to be sampled in the current step are determined before any computation, allowing them to be sampled jointly . Let T ⊆ { 1 , … , N } T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\} denote the masked positions to be sampled jointly in the same step, with values 𝒙 T := { x j } j ∈ T \bm{x}_{T}:=\{x^{j}\}_{j\in T} . sections.heading: 4.5 Fine-Tuning Pretrained MDMs and Implementation Details
sections.text: Our tensor-decomposition framework can be integrated into pretrained MDMs via fine-tuning. We describe the necessary architectural modifications and other implementation details below. Figure 2: Architectural modifications for fine-tuning MDMs.

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: A standard MDM produces N ​ V NV logits, but tensor-decomposed forms require E ​ V ​ N EVN , where E = r E=r (CPD; plus r r rank weights) or E = r 2 E=r^{2} (TTD). Our 1-layer method replaces the final head 𝑾 ∈ ℝ H × V \bm{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times V} with 𝑾 ′ ∈ ℝ H × E ​ V \bm{W}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times EV} , which is costly for large V V . Following Basharin et al. (2025) , the 2-layer method instead inserts 𝑾 ~ ∈ ℝ H × E ​ H \widetilde{\bm{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times EH} before the final head, then applies 𝑾 \bm{W} to each of the E E outputs, which significantly reduces the parameter count since H ≪ V H\ll V in language models. sections.heading: 5.2 Molecule Generation
sections.text: We evaluate on the molecule generation task using QM9 ( Blum and Reymond, 2009 ; Rupp et al., 2012 ) , with MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , parameterized using DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , as the base model. Given the smaller vocabulary size ( V = 40 V=40 ) relative to text generation, a 1-layer architecture suffices, with r CPD = 64 , r TTD = 8 r_{\text{CPD}}=64,r_{\text{TTD}}=8 . Training and sampling details are described in App. D.2 . For the DiT architecture, we modify the rotary positional encoding to apply the rotary matrices to values as well. We stress that this is crucial for any MDM-like sampling methods. Without such a modification, the first sampling step collapses entirely for both the baseline MDLM and our methods due to the uniformity of the inputs in every position. The necessity of such a modification is proved in App. C . Figure 3: Molecule generation on QM9 ( Blum and Reymond, 2009 ; Rupp et al., 2012 ) . The proposed method consistently achieves higher validity than baselines, including few-step regimes. We evaluate each method by sampling 1024 molecules with random ordering across varying numbers of sampling steps, then compute validity, and uniqueness and novelty among valid samples. These metrics are summarized in Fig. 3 . We find that our methods bring significant improvements despite small increases in model size. Additional experiments, including sampling strategy comparisons and rank size ablations, are provided in App. E.1 . We observe that, as predicted from our discussion in Sec. 4 , TTD outperforms CPD of the same output size, and that this gap is the largest in left-to-right generation, where the structural bias of TTD can be exploited to the fullest extent.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented the first framework for explicit joint distribution modeling in discrete diffusion, parameterizing the conditional clean distribution p 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) as a low-rank tensor via CPD or TTD and thus generalizing standard MDMs. Our analysis identifies a structural bias of TTD toward dependencies between nearby tokens, making it particularly well-suited to sequential data. Through an efficient sampling procedure and a lightweight fine-tuning recipe, the framework integrates with any base MDM or latent-variable method and substantially improves few-step generation on both text and molecule benchmarks.

sections.heading: Societal Impacts
sections.text: This work targets efficiency improvements for discrete diffusion generation. On the positive side, faster sampling can reduce the computational cost and energy use of sequential generation, and may accelerate beneficial downstream applications such as molecular design and biological sequence modeling. As with any advance in generative model efficiency, there is also potential for misuse (e.g., faster generation of misleading textual content), though such risks are inherent to the broader generative modeling paradigm rather than introduced by our framework.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: A fundamental challenge in discrete diffusion modeling is that the joint distribution p 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}|\bm{x}_{t}) over N N tokens corresponds to an N N -dimensional tensor with V N V^{N} entries. For arbitrary target distributions this tensor can be of prohibitively high rank, so any tractable parameterization, including ours, must rely on a low-rank approximation, and arbitrarily increasing the rank in CPD or TTD is infeasible in practice. Nonetheless, our experiments show that even low ranks yield substantial few-step improvements across both text and molecule generation, indicating that low-rank structure suffices in the regime where parallelization bias is most severe. As future work, we plan to explore richer tensor formats, such as Tucker decomposition, which may capture dependency structures beyond the locality bias of TTD and offer alternative trade-offs between rank and expressivity.

sections.heading: Appendix C A Pitfall of RoPE in Masked Diffusion
sections.text: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [ Su et al., 2024 ] incorporates positional information into the attention layer by "rotating" queries and keys by q m = R Θ , m d ​ W q ​ x m , k n = R Θ , n d ​ W k ​ x n q_{m}=R^{d}_{\Theta,m}W_{q}x_{m},k_{n}=R^{d}_{\Theta,n}W_{k}x_{n} where R Θ , m d R^{d}_{\Theta,m} and R Θ , n d R^{d}_{\Theta,n} are appropriately defined rotary matrices. (Here we write position indices in subscripts to match Su et al. [2024] .) This method, however, should be used with care on MDMs. In the very first step of MDM generation, the input is a fully-masked sequence. Since default RoPE neither changes the token embeddings nor the values in attention layers, it loses its ability to distinguish between positions. If the initial x m = x x_{m}=x is uniform across position, v m = W v ​ x m = W v ​ x = v v_{m}=W_{v}x_{m}=W_{v}x=v is also uniform, and thus the output of attention layer o m = ∑ n = 1 N a m , n ​ v n = v ​ ∑ n = 1 N a m , n = v \displaystyle o_{m}=\sum\limits_{n=1}^{N}a_{m,n}v_{n}=v\sum\limits_{n=1}^{N}a_{m,n}=v (27) also becomes uniform regardless of the attention weights a a . All the other components, such as normalizing layers or dense layers, are applied independently to each position, maintaining this unintended uniformity. Indeed, we confirm that under this formulation, the outputted logits of the model are identical for every position in the first step. Although this issue is less pronounced in settings such as conditional generation (where the first step is not fully masked), long sequence generation (where the impact of an incorrectly chosen first token is negligible), or datasets where true marginal probabilities are similar across positions, we observed noticeable performance degradation in our QM9 [ Blum and Reymond, 2009 , Rupp et al., 2012 ] experiments, where the model performs unconditional generation of short sequences. This motivated a fix: applying RoPE rotary matrices to values in addition to queries and keys in attention. Note that we retain the previous behavior in Sec. 5.1 for compatibility with the pretrained model.

sections.heading: D.1 Text Generation
sections.text: For OWT [ Gokaslan et al., 2019 ] and LM1B [ Chelba et al., 2014 ] , we matched the training time for each method. Each resulted in a total training time of approximately 10 hours on four NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. For MDLM [ Sahoo et al., 2024 ] we fine-tuned the base model with global batch size 64, constant learning rate 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} with Adam for 100k steps, and for CPD and TTD we used global batch size 4 for 150k steps. Di4C [ Hayakawa et al., 2025 ] model was trained for 13k steps with the base model as the teacher model, with other hyperparameters set to default values in the released code of global batch size 4 and constant learning rate 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} with warmup for 2500 steps with AdamW [ Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ] optimizer, alongside exponential moving average (EMA) with decay rate of 0.9999. For EDLM [ Xu et al., 2025 ] , we used the checkpoints from MDLM with the AR-based method, and used the default sampling parameter of sampling size k = 2 k=2 but widened the sampling window to w = 1 w=1 to follow the setting outlined in their paper. For DCD [ Liu et al., 2025 ] , we followed the released code and used sedd-medium [ Lou et al., 2024 ] as the diffusion model and gpt2 [ Radford et al., 2019 ] as the AR model with a chunk size of 1 to simulate fully random generation. For VADD [ Xie et al., 2026 ] , we trained the base model with the default values in the released code of global batch size 512 and constant learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} with warmup for 2500 steps with AdamW and EMA with decay rate 0.9999 for 5k steps on latent dimension of 512. VADD and our methods were fine-tuned from the base model in the same setting, with VADD for 1k steps and our methods for 400 steps. For sampling we followed their default setting using fixed latent. For measuring the sampling times, we generated 64 sequences with 128 timesteps on batch size of 1 for every method and computed the sampling time of a single sequence. Sampling time measurements were conducted on a single NVIDIA PRO6000 GPU.

sections.heading: D.2 Molecule Generation
sections.text: The base MDLM [ Sahoo et al., 2024 ] was trained with global batch size 8192, constant learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} with Adam [ Kingma and Ba, 2015 ] for 50k steps. For MDLM and our methods, we fine-tuned the base model under the same settings for 10k steps. Di4C [ Hayakawa et al., 2025 ] model was trained for 10k steps with our base model as the teacher model, with global batch size 512 and other hyperparameters set to default values in the released code of constant learning rate 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} with warmup for 2500 steps with AdamW [ Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ] and exponential moving average (EMA) with decay rate 0.9999. VADD [ Xie et al., 2026 ] model was trained for 60k steps from scratch with global batch size 2048 and other hyperparameters set to default values in the released code of constant learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} with warmup for 2500 steps with AdamW and EMA with decay rate 0.9999 on latent dimension of 512. For sampling of VADD we also followed their default setting using fixed latent. Experiments were conducted using four GPUs of either NVIDIA A6000 or PRO6000.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.03788v1 [cs.LG] 04 Jul 2026 Tensor-Train Joint Modeling for Few-Step Masked Diffusion Byoungkwon Kim Affiliation: KAIST Email: ssamt@kaist.ac.kr Minhyuk Sung Affiliation: KAIST Email: mhsung@kaist.ac.kr Abstract Discrete diffusion promises orders-of-magnitude faster generation than autoregressive (AR) models for sequential discrete data, yet its full potential of few-step generation has remained out of reach due to a fundamental structural limitation. The conditional-independence assumption underlying current discrete diffusion models introduces a systematic parallelization bias that compounds with the number of tokens unmasked per step, becoming severe in the few-step regime that fast generation requires. We address this with the first framework for explicit joint distribution modeling in discrete diffusion via tensor decomposition , which represents the conditional clean distribution as a low-rank tensor with controllable expressivity. The framework supports both Canonical Polyadic (CPD) and Tensor-Train (TTD) decompositions, and we identify a structural bias of TTD toward dependencies between nearby tokens, formalized through Oseledets’ theorem relating TT-rank to unfolding-matrix rank, which is well-suited to sequential data such as natural language and line notations for molecular data. To enable efficient generation, we present an iterative marginal inference procedure with specialization for predetermined position schedules. Our framework integrates into pretrained MDMs through lightweight fine-tuning, yielding substantial improvements in few-step generation at a fraction of the cost of training from scratch. 1 Introduction Discrete diffusion has emerged as a compelling alternative to AR models for generating sequential discrete data such as text and proteins ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Its key promise is parallel token generation, producing multiple tokens per step rather than one. Most notably, Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) have scaled to large language models ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) with competitive quality and faster generation. In practice, however, this speed potential remains unrealized, as pushing toward few-step generation systematically degrades sample quality. The root cause is structural; to remain tractable, discrete diffusion models represent the conditional clean distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{	heta}( m{x}| m{x}_{t}) under the conditional-independence assumption p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) = ∏ i = 1 N p θ ​ ( x i | 𝒙 t ) p_{	heta}( m{x}| m{x}_{t})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{	heta}(x^{i}| m{x}_{t}) . This assumption introduces a systematic parallelization bias ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) when multiple tokens are unmasked simultaneously. The bias compounds with the number of tokens unmasked per step, becoming especially severe in the few-step regime that fast generation requires. Resolving this bias requires modeling the joint distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{	heta}( m{x}| m{x}_{t}) explicitly. However, naïve joint modeling is infeasible since the joint over N N tokens with vocabulary size V V forms an N N -dimensional tensor with V N V^{N} entries. Some existing approaches therefore sidestep direct joint modeling, introducing latent factors that induce token correlations ( Hayakawa et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) or borrowing dependence from auxiliary autoregressive models ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Compared to AR-auxiliary approaches, our method models the joint distribution explicitly as a tractable parametric family within the discrete diffusion model itself, without requiring any external pretrained model. Also, compared to latent-variable approaches, our explicit parameterization is orthogonal to their implicit one, and the two can be combined for further gains. Concurrent work ( Li et al., 2026 ) addresses the same factorization barrier by augmenting the factorized neural output with a tractable probabilistic circuit prior, requiring manual structural design for sequential locality, whereas Tensor-Train decomposition provides the same tractability with a theoretically grounded locality bias. In this work, we introduce a framework that explicitly parameterizes the joint distribution p θ ​ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 t ) p_{	heta}( m{x}| m{x}_{t}) via tensor decomposition ( Kolda and Bader, 2009 ) . Compared to prior work, our framework provides explicit joint modeling within the diffusion model itself, without relying on auxiliary models. Our contributions are four-fold. • First explicit joint modeling via tensor decomposition. To our knowledge, this is the first work to parameterize the conditional clean distribution of discrete diffusion via tensor decomposition, strictly generalizing standard MDMs as the rank-one case. • TTD for sequential structure. We develop the framework for both Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) ( Hitchcock, 1927 ) and Tensor-Train Decomposition (TTD) ( Oseledets, 2011 ) , identifying a structural bias of TTD toward dependencies between nearby tokens, formalized through Oseledets’ theorem relating TT-rank to unfolding-matrix rank. • Efficient sampling via marginal inference. Direct sampling from a joint of size V N V^{N} is intractable. We present a chain-rule procedure built on iterative marginal inference via caching and parallel prefix sums, with specialization for predetermined position schedules. • Lightweight fine-tuning of pretrained MDMs. Our framework integrates into pretrained MDMs through small architectural modifications initialized to preserve the marginal predictions, yielding substantial few-step improvements at a fraction of the cost of training from scratch. In experiments on text generation (OpenWebText ( Gokaslan et al., 2019 ) , LM1B ( Chelba et al., 2014 ) ) and molecule generation (QM9 ( Blum and Reymond, 2009 ; Rupp et al., 2012 ) ), our framework delivers substantial few-step improvements across multiple base models, including MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) and VADD ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . As predicted by our theory, TTD consistently outperforms CPD on these sequential domains, with the largest gains concentrated in the few-step regime. For instance, TTD-based fine-tuning of VADD reduces 8-step generative perplexity on OpenWebText by 32.7% over vanilla VADD, while being only 1.7% slower at 128 timesteps. 2 Related Work Several lines of work attempt to address the parallelization bias arising from the conditional-independence assumption in discrete diffusion. The central challenge is the exponential size of the joint distribution: an N N -token sequence over vocabulary V V admits V N V^{N} possible configurations, making direct modeling intractable. Auxiliary-model approaches distill dependency information from separately trained autoregressive models via copula-based reweighting ( Liu et al., 2025 ) or energy-based reweighting ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . While effective, these methods inherit the inference cost of an external model and become inapplicable in domains lacking strong AR models, such as generation of line notations for molecular data. Our framework, in contrast, requires no additional model. Latent-variable approaches introduce latent factors that induce token correlations through marginalization, either via a continuous mixing variable ( Hayakawa et al., 2025 ) or a VAE-style latent vector ( Xie et al., 2026 ) ; our explicit modeling is orthogonal to these implicit approaches and can be combined with them for further gains. Sampling strategies mitigate the bias without modifying the model, selecting positions via low-discrepancy schedules ( Besnier et al., 2025 ) or adaptively bounding the number of simultaneously unmasked tokens through entropy criteria ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2025 ) ; these strategies integrate naturally within our framework. Concurrent work ( Li et al., 2026 ) couples the factorized neural output with a tractable probabilistic circuit prior, addressing the same factorization barrier with a different parameterization. Although probabilistic circuits offer general-purpose tractable inference, they require manual structural design for sequential locality, whereas Tensor-Train decomposition provides the same tractability with a theoretically grounded locality bias ( Sec. 4.2 ), making it particularly suited to natural language and line notations for molecular data without further structural engineering. The parallelization bias has also been studied in the context of speculative decoding for autoregressive language models, where Basharin et al. (2025) were the first to apply Canonical Polyadic Decomposition for explicit token-wise dependency modeling.
